nameStory: The Lesser Scaup gets its unusual name from the Scottish word 'scalp,' referring to the clams, oysters, and mussels this diving duck loves to eat. Some folks think it might come from the female's harsh 'scaup' call instead. Either way, it's also called the 'little bluebill' for its distinctive bright blue bill that catches the eye from across the water.
description: The Lesser Scaup is a small diving duck that visits New England waters during migration and winter. Males sport a glossy black head with a purple sheen, white sides, and a black back, while females are brownish with a white patch around the bill base. Both sexes have that telltale bright blue bill that gives them their nickname 'bluebill.' These compact ducks are excellent divers, disappearing underwater to hunt for shellfish and aquatic plants.

idTips.label: Blue Bill
idTips.description: Both males and females have a distinctive bright blue bill that stands out like a beacon against the water - you can spot this blue from surprisingly far away

idTips.label: Male Head Shape
idTips.description: Males have a rounded, not peaked, head with glossy black feathers that show purple highlights in good light - the head looks smooth and dome-like

idTips.label: Female Markings
idTips.description: Females are warm brown overall with a distinctive white patch at the base of their blue bill that looks like they dipped their face in paint

idTips.label: Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch them completely disappear underwater for 10-25 seconds while feeding - they don't just tip forward like mallards but vanish entirely beneath the surface

idTips.label: Flock Formation
idTips.description: Often seen in tight groups on open water, sometimes forming 'rafts' of dozens of birds that move together like a floating carpet

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: In flight, shows a white stripe along the wing that's shorter than their Greater Scaup cousins - extends only partway across the wing

habitat: Look for Lesser Scaup on larger bodies of open water including coastal bays, harbors, lakes, and reservoirs throughout New England. They prefer deeper waters where they can dive for food, often gathering in sheltered coves and harbors along the coast. During migration, they might turn up on inland lakes and ponds, especially larger ones with minimal shoreline vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs from March through May as flocks move north to breeding grounds. Males are in their sharpest breeding plumage with glossy black heads and bright white sides.
seasonality.summer: Most birds have moved north to breed, though a few non-breeding individuals might linger on coastal waters. Any summer sightings are noteworthy.
seasonality.fall: Return migration begins in October and November, with mixed flocks of males, females, and young birds. Males may look duller as they molt into winter plumage.
seasonality.winter: Peak abundance from December through February on coastal waters and ice-free inland lakes. Both sexes present but males in duller winter plumage with less contrast.

funFact: Lesser Scaup can dive down to 25 feet underwater and have been found with their stomachs completely packed with tiny zebra mussels - sometimes containing over 100 of these invasive shellfish in a single meal, making them unlikely heroes in controlling these aquatic pests.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Greater Scaup, but Lesser Scaup have rounder heads (not peaked), shorter white wing stripes in flight, and slightly smaller size. Memory trick: 'Lesser has Less white on the wing.' Ring-necked Ducks have white rings around their bills and different head shapes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Lesser,' these aren't necessarily smaller than all their relatives - the name simply distinguishes them from Greater Scaup. The 'bluebill' nickname is shared with Greater Scaup, which can cause confusion among duck hunters and birders when people don't specify which species they're discussing.
compareHints: Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes. Ring-necked Ducks have peaked heads and white bill rings rather than all-blue bills. Redheads and Canvasbacks are larger with different head colors - rusty red rather than black in males.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring.
Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back.

Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups.
Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes.
